about.title: About Revert Guide
about.mission: Revert Guide helps people through their first year as a Muslim. That first year holds a lot of questions, and most of them are ordinary ones nobody wants to feel embarrassed asking. So the answers live here in one place, they work offline, and they cost nothing.

approachItems.title: Educational and beginner-focused
approachItems.body: We explain concepts from scratch, assuming no prior knowledge of Islam.

approachItems.title: Mainstream Sunni perspective
approachItems.body: The content and the masjid directory follow mainstream Sunni scholarship, without sectarian argument. Where the four Sunni schools of law differ, we say so and do not pick one for you.

approachItems.title: Non-political and inclusive
approachItems.body: We stick to faith and practice, and welcome Muslims from every cultural background.

approachItems.title: Essentials over advanced topics
approachItems.body: We cover the fundamentals new Muslims need most, and leave advanced jurisprudence to scholars.

approachItems.title: Ad-free and non-commercial
approachItems.body: No ads, no trackers, no monetization. This is a service, not a business.

approachItems.title: Complementary to local guidance
approachItems.body: Find a local mosque and a mentor. This guide adds to those relationships, it does not stand in for them.

about.whoRunsBody: Revert Guide is a volunteer project. It is not a business, it carries no ads, and it does not sell anything.
about.reviewIntro: Every page moves through four stages.

reviewStates.name: Draft
reviewStates.body: The page is written, but nobody has checked its sources yet.

reviewStates.name: Source-checked
reviewStates.body: Someone on the team has opened every source the page cites and confirmed it says what the page says.

reviewStates.name: Review needed
reviewStates.body: The sources are checked, but the page touches rulings, health, safety, law or family matters, so it is waiting for a qualified reviewer.

reviewStates.name: Approved
reviewStates.body: A qualified reviewer has read the page and signed it off.

about.badgeTitle: If a page says review needed
about.badgeBody: You can still use it. The information is sourced, but a qualified reviewer has not signed it off yet. For anything about your own situation, check with a local imam, scholar or the right professional.
about.reviewerBody: Religious content is reviewed by a qualified reviewer approved by the team. We will publish the reviewer roster once it is confirmed.
about.disclaimer: This guide gives general educational information about Islam. It is not a substitute for a personal religious ruling (fatwa). For questions about your own situation, ask a knowledgeable local scholar or imam. We aim for accuracy, and any errors here are unintentional.
about.contact: For questions about Islam itself, a local masjid or mentor can answer you in person, and that is better than anything a website can do. To reach our team, ask for a mentor, report a mistake or tell us about an accessibility problem, use the Get help page or email us.

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.commitment: Revert Guide is built to work for people of every ability. The site meets WCAG 2.1 Level AA criteria and the requirements of the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA). Nobody should be shut out of this content by the way it was coded.

policySections.title: The short version
paragraphs: You can read everything on Revert Guide without an account. We do not use analytics, ads or tracking cookies, and we collect nothing about you while you browse.
The only time our team receives personal information is when you choose to send us a help request. This policy covers the two situations separately.

policySections.title: When you browse
paragraphs: Reading the site sends nothing about you to our team. There are no accounts, no analytics and no advertising.

So that the site works offline, your browser saves pages on your own device. We cannot see this. Someone else who uses your device may be able to see which pages you visited, and clearing your browsing data removes them.

A few tools have to contact another service to work. Each of those services receives standard request data, such as your IP address and browser type, plus whatever the tool sends. They are listed in the next section.

policySections.title: Other services, tool by tool
paragraphs: This is every outside service the site can contact, and when.

items.label: Find a masjid, map:
items.text: Map images come from OpenStreetMap. The OpenStreetMap Foundation logs request data such as your IP address, browser and the page that asked for the map, and keeps detailed usage information for 180 days.

items.label: Find a masjid, address search:
items.text: What you type is sent to Nominatim, the OpenStreetMap search service, along with your IP address. A postal code or neighbourhood works as well as a street address, so you never need to type your home address.

items.label: Find a masjid, use my location:
items.text: This button is optional. Your browser asks your permission first. Your location is used on your device to sort the list, and this site never sends it to our team or to any server.

items.label: Qibla direction:
items.text: The Qibla page asks your browser for your location and works out the direction on your device. The site sends your location nowhere. To find where you are, your browser or phone may use its own location service. Wi-Fi positioning, for example, is often provided by Google.

items.label: Prayer times:
items.text: The address or city you type is sent to AlAdhan, a free prayer times service run by Islamic Network, along with your IP address. We could not find a published privacy policy for AlAdhan. Typing a city instead of a street address keeps this more private.

items.label: The 99 names of Allah:
items.text: This page loads the names from AlAdhan. It sends no address, only standard request data such as your IP address.

items.label: Videos:
items.text: Videos use YouTube's privacy-enhanced player. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press play. Once you press play, YouTube receives standard request data such as your IP address, and it may set cookies or store similar data on your device. YouTube says views in this mode are not used to personalise your YouTube experience or the ads you see elsewhere. If you click through to YouTube itself, YouTube's own privacy policy applies.

items.label: WhatsApp:
items.text: If you follow our WhatsApp Channel, other followers cannot see your phone number, and only admins who have saved you as a contact can see it. A WhatsApp group is different. Joining one shows your phone number to the group admins, and other members may see it too. WhatsApp's own terms apply to both.

items.label: Links to other websites:
items.text: Websites we link to have their own privacy practices, which we do not control.

policySections.title: When you ask us for help
paragraphs: The help form on the Get help page is the one place we collect personal information. It asks only what we need to reply to you or to find you support: the kind of help you want, your language, how you would like us to contact you, and your city or province. You can use a nickname.

The form is a Google Form. We link to it instead of placing it on our pages, so nothing from Google loads until you open it. We set it up so you do not need to sign in to a Google account. Your answers are stored in our team's Google account, and Google receives standard request data such as your IP address. Google may set cookies on the form page, and it may store data outside Canada.
Please do not include anything you would not want stored online.
If you email us instead, your message is kept in our email inbox.

policySections.title: Who can read your request
paragraphs: One or two coordinators read requests in one shared inbox. If you ask for a mentor, we pass on only the details the mentor needs, and only after you agree. We do not sell requests or share them with anyone else.

policySections.title: How long we keep it
paragraphs: We aim to reply within 48 to 72 hours. After that, a request stays open only while we are helping you.
Our target is to delete a help request 6 months after it is closed. The team will confirm the exact period and update this page. You can ask us to delete your request at any time, and we will.

policySections.title: Your consent
paragraphs: A help request tells us that you are Muslim, new to Islam, or thinking about it. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada treats religious belief as sensitive information and says organisations should generally get express consent before collecting it.

The form tells you what we collect, who sees it, why we need it and the risks, and asks you to agree before you send it. Sending the form is your consent for us to use your answers to reply to you and to arrange the help you asked for. You can withdraw that consent by asking us to delete your request.

policySections.title: If you are keeping your conversion private
paragraphs: Browsing Revert Guide sends nothing about you to our team. What others could see is on your own device: your browsing history and the pages saved for offline reading. A private or incognito window keeps pages out of your history.
What you type into the prayer times tool or the masjid search goes to the services listed above.

A help request does leave your device, and goes to Google and to our team as described above. You can send the form from another device, such as a library computer or a trusted friend's phone, and give a contact method that only you check.

policySections.title: Children's privacy
paragraphs: This site is not directed to children under 13, and we do not knowingly collect information from them.

policySections.title: Changes to this policy
paragraphs: If we update this policy, the new version goes on this page and the effective date at the top changes with it. Check back now and then.

policySections.title: Contact
paragraphs: For questions about this policy, or to ask us to delete a help request, contact us through the Get help page or by email.

For personal religious decisions, consult a qualified local scholar or imam. We aim for accuracy but cannot guarantee every detail is error-free, so use the content at your own discretion.

You may read the site and share links to it, but not republish, copy, modify, or redistribute the content without permission. sources.howToUseTitle: How to use sources without feeling overwhelmed
sources.howToUseBody: You do not need to become an expert in checking sources. Start with the basics, learn from teachers you trust, and ask someone qualified when a question touches your worship, your family, your health, or your money. The tags are here so you can check our work. They are not one more thing you have to master.
sources.endorsementNote: A source tag does not mean that organisation endorses Revert Guide. It shows where we looked for supporting information and where you can keep reading.

ramadan.title: Ramadan guide
ramadan.subtitle: Your first Ramadan as a Muslim.

whatIsRamadan.title: What is Ramadan?
whatIsRamadan.body: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar and the month Muslims fast. From dawn until sunset you take no food, no drink, and no intimacy. The fasting is the visible part, but the month is also about prayer, reading Quran, giving, and paying closer attention to how you treat people. The first revelation of the Quran came during Ramadan, which is part of why the month carries the weight it does.

forNewMuslims.title: For new Muslims
forNewMuslims.calloutBody: If this is your first Ramadan, feeling anxious or unsure about it is normal. Whatever fasting you manage counts, and you can build up from there. Go easy on yourself. Muslims who have fasted their whole lives still find some days hard.
forNewMuslims.body: Find a fasting buddy, a mentor, or a community group so you are not doing the month alone. Many mosques run programs specifically for new Muslims during Ramadan, and most people are glad to be asked.
forNewMuslims.convertedLinkLabel: Became Muslim during Ramadan? What you owe and what you do not

items.desc: is the meal before dawn. Eat something steady before the Fajr prayer, because it carries you through the day. Fibre and protein keep you full longer than sugar does.
is the meal that breaks the fast at sunset, traditionally dates and water first. That was the practice of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and it gets energy back into you quickly.
is food, drink, and intimacy from dawn to sunset. If you eat or drink by accident, the fast still stands. Just stop and carry on.
includes anyone who is ill, traveling, elderly, pregnant, nursing, or menstruating. Missed days can be made up later.
is made in your heart, either the night before or before dawn, that you are fasting for the sake of Allah.

preparing.title: Preparing for Ramadan
items: Shift your sleep earlier over a few days, since you will be up before dawn for suhoor.
Cut back on caffeine beforehand so you are not fasting through a withdrawal headache.
Decide on simple suhoor and iftar meals in advance, before you are tired and hungry.
Tell your employer or school if it helps. Most people are reasonable about religious observance.
Learn two short supplications: the intention for fasting, and the dua for breaking it.
Pick one or two goals for the month, such as reading more Quran, giving regularly, or repairing a relationship.
Set a little money aside for Eid, zakat al-fitr and gifts ahead of time, so the end of the month does not land on a credit card.

duringRamadan.title: During Ramadan
spiritualPractices: Read some Quran daily. Ramadan is the month of the Quran, and a few verses a day still counts.
Pray more, especially Tarawih at the mosque at night.
Make dua often. The supplication of someone fasting carries particular weight.
Give sadaqah if you can. Generosity is strongly encouraged this month.
duringRamadan.practicalTipsCalloutBody: Drink plenty of water between iftar and suhoor. Dehydration causes more trouble than hunger does, especially during long summer fasts.
practicalTips: Do not skip suhoor. It is the difference between a manageable day and a miserable one.
Nap if you can, particularly when Tarawih and suhoor are cutting into your sleep.
Expect to flag in the afternoon, so put demanding work in the morning where possible.
Break your fast with dates and water. It follows the Sunnah and gets energy back fast.

tarawihAndCommunity.title: Night prayers and community (tarawih)
tarawihAndCommunity.tarawihBodyBeforeIsha: Tarawih are the extra evening prayers held during Ramadan, after
tarawihAndCommunity.tarawihBodyAfterIsha: (Isha) prayer at the mosque. They run long, and leaving partway through is fine. Try to go at least once, because the room during Tarawih is something you have to be in to understand.
tarawihAndCommunity.iftarBody: Iftar gatherings at mosques and community centers are an easy way to break your fast with other people. There is usually far more food than anyone expects and someone who will introduce themselves. For a lot of converts these evenings are where the first real friendships start.
tarawihAndCommunity.calloutBody: Find a fasting buddy or a mentor for the month. Having one person who knows how your week is going makes the whole thing lighter.

laylatAlQadr.title: Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power)
laylatAlQadr.body: Through the last ten nights of Ramadan, Muslims look for Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power. The Quran calls it better than a thousand months. Nobody knows the exact date, so it is traditionally sought on the odd nights of those ten: the 21st, 23rd, 25th, 27th, or 29th. Many people pray more, read more Quran, and stay up later during this stretch.

eidAlFitr.title: The festival after Ramadan (Eid al-Fitr)
eidAlFitr.body: Eid al-Fitr is the celebration at the end of Ramadan. It starts with the Eid prayer in the morning, usually in a large gathering at a mosque or in an open space.
items: Wear your best clothes and greet people with "Eid Mubarak", meaning blessed Eid.
Eat with your community. Eid is a day for celebrating and being grateful.
If you can, give Zakat al-Fitr, a small charitable payment, before the Eid prayer. Your mosque can tell you the amount.
eidAlFitr.calloutBody: Feeling emotional on Eid is common, especially when your family is far away or does not understand what you are celebrating. You have a community now. Go to the prayer, eat too much, and be proud of the month you just completed.

ramadan.planningBody: Use these short checklists as a starting point. Ramadan runs a whole month, so there is no need to do everything in the first week.
ramadan.careBody: These notes are here to get you oriented. Your own fasting case needs qualified religious review, and anything touching your health needs medical advice as well.
ramadan.sourcesNote: The worship material here rests on Quran and hadith references, and the practical framing comes from beginner education sources. Ask a qualified local imam about illness, travel, menstruation, medication, fidyah, or missed fasts.
ramadan.checklistAlt: My first Ramadan, a checklist with empty tick boxes. Before Ramadan: ask your masjid how they announce the start; learn the basics, no food, drink or intimacy from dawn to sunset; know who is excused and ask about your own case. Each day: eat something at suhoor before dawn; break the fast soon after sunset with water or dates; pick one small act of worship you can keep. Along the way: try taraweeh once if you like, it is optional; tell one person how it is going. Missing a day or struggling does not undo your Ramadan. Allah wants ease for you.
ramadan.checklistCaption: A printable checklist for your first Ramadan. Tick what helps and leave the rest.
ramadan.sistersLinkLabel: Sisters: what changes during your period

mentalHealth.title: Taking care of your mind
mentalHealth.subtitle: How you are doing emotionally matters. This page is here for that.

validation.title: Your feelings are valid
validation.calloutBody: Plenty of new Muslims deal with loneliness, doubt, anxiety, questions about who they are now, or conflict at home. None of that makes you a bad Muslim. It makes you a person.
validation.body: Becoming Muslim is one of the largest decisions a person can make. It is a good one, and it is still a major life change that takes an emotional toll while you adjust. Feeling overwhelmed or conflicted some weeks is ordinary. What matters is that you are here and still learning. Converts before you have gone through the same stretch and come out the other side of it.

faithAndHelp.title: Faith and professional help
paragraphs: Islam teaches mercy, and it treats caring for your mind as part of caring for yourself. Trust in Allah is a real comfort, and the same faith tells us to take practical means as well. We see a doctor for a physical illness and pray for healing at the same time. Seeing a counselor for emotional distress works exactly the same way.

The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his companions felt grief, sadness, and stress. Being Muslim does not mean being happy every moment. It means holding onto hope and carrying on through the hard parts.
faithAndHelp.calloutBody: There is a well-known saying: tie your camel, then trust in Allah. Do the practical thing about your problem, and put your trust in God alongside it. Therapy is one of those practical things.

items.title: Loneliness
items.body: You may feel isolated if you have no Muslim friends yet, or if your family has pulled back. This part does pass, even though it does not feel that way while you are in it.
items.help: Join a new Muslim class or a community event at your local mosque. Online groups help when nothing in-person is available. Ask whether your mosque runs a convert support group, because many of them do.

items.title: Family conflict
items.body: Your family may not understand why you converted, and some will react with confusion, worry, or anger. For a lot of converts this is the hardest part of the whole thing.
items.help: Keep talking to them warmly where you can. Give them time to adjust, and skip the debates about every detail of the faith. Set gentle boundaries to protect your own peace. Other converts have been through this and can tell you what worked.

items.title: Identity questions
items.body: You may feel caught between who you were and who you are now. Wondering whether you are "Muslim enough", or feeling like a fraud in a religious setting, is very common.
items.help: You do not have to throw out your culture or your personality to be Muslim. Islam adds to who you are. It does not delete who you were. Keep the good from how you were raised and let it sit alongside your faith. There is no single correct way to be Muslim, and nobody is on a schedule.

items.title: Doubts in faith
items.body: You may have doubts about Islam, or second-guess the decision entirely. Faith rises and falls, and questions come with any serious commitment.
items.help: Islam tells you to go looking for knowledge. Talk to a mentor who knows the material, read reliable books, or sit in on a study circle. Do not bottle the questions up. Working through them honestly usually leaves faith stronger than it was. Make dua for guidance, and give yourself time.

items.title: Ramadan and eating disorders
items.body: If you have an eating disorder, or are recovering from one, Ramadan can be a hard month. Fasting can make restriction look normal, hide a relapse, or lead to bingeing at iftar. An eating disorder is an illness, and the illness exemption from fasting covers it.
items.help: Talk to your treatment team before you decide anything about fasting, and ask a scholar privately about your own case. You do not have to prove your faith by fasting against medical advice. You can take part in Ramadan through prayer, Quran, dua, giving and helping at iftar. NEDIC's helpline is listed under support resources below.

selfCare.title: Practical self-care
items: Cover the basics: enough sleep, decent food, some movement. Physical state drives emotional state more than most people expect.
Stay in touch with a friend or mentor. Even one call a week changes things.
Do things that settle you, whether that is a walk outside, reading, or making something. Enjoying yourself is not un-Islamic.
Use dhikr and prayer when anxiety spikes. Repeating "SubhanAllah", or reciting Al-Fatiha, can steady a bad moment.
Write your feelings down, or say them in dua. Getting them out of your head relieves the pressure.
Set boundaries with people and situations that drain you. Protecting your peace is not selfish.
Slow your breathing. Dhikr works well for this, since repeating "SubhanAllah" on long breaths calms the body and the heart together.
Find a community or a mentor who understands what converting is like. You are not meant to do this by yourself.

seekHelp.title: When to seek professional help
seekHelp.intro: If any of the following describes you, contact a mental health professional or a crisis line. Needing help is not weak faith. Islam supports getting treatment, and asking for it takes more courage than going without.
items: Sadness, hopelessness, or emptiness that persists and does not lift
Not being able to manage daily things like eating, working, or washing, because of how you feel
Panic attacks, or anxiety intense enough to interfere with daily life
Thoughts of harming yourself, or wishing you were not alive
Feeling completely unable to cope
Using substances to get through the day
seekHelp.calloutTitle: If you are in immediate danger
seekHelp.calloutBody: If you are thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8 at any hour. If you are in immediate danger, call 9-1-1 or go to the nearest emergency department now. Your life matters.

disclaimer.label: Note:
disclaimer.body: This guide offers general emotional support and education. It is not a substitute for therapy or medical advice. If you are in a mental health crisis, contact a licensed professional or one of the crisis resources below.

resources.title: Support resources
resources.confidentialityNote: Helplines keep what you tell them confidential. Some, including Kids Help Phone, say they may contact emergency services if someone's life is in danger.

supportGroups.title: If you are in danger or thinking about suicide

items.name: Emergency services (9-1-1)
items.desc: If you or someone else is in immediate danger or needs urgent medical help, call 9-1-1 or go to the nearest emergency department.

items.name: 9-8-8: Suicide Crisis Helpline
items.desc: For anyone in Canada who is thinking about suicide, or who is worried about someone else. Free, 24 hours a day.

items.name: Kids Help Phone
items.desc: Free 24/7 support for young people across Canada. Texts are confidential but not anonymous.

items.name: Hope for Wellness Help Line
items.desc: 24/7 counselling and crisis support for First Nations, Inuit and Métis people anywhere in Canada.

items.name: Naseeha helpline
items.desc: A 24/7 helpline for Muslim youth, run by a Canadian Muslim charity. It is not an emergency service. If your life is in danger, call 9-1-1 or 9-8-8 first.

supportGroups.title: Women's services
supportGroups.intro: Services run by Muslim charities for women and girls. If you are in immediate danger, call 9-1-1.

items.name: Sakeenah Canada emergency hotline
items.desc: A 24/7 hotline for women and children fleeing domestic violence, run by a Canadian Muslim charity. Sakeenah also runs transitional homes in several Canadian cities.

items.name: Nisa Helpline
items.desc: Free, confidential peer support for Muslim women and girls aged 14 and up, 7 days a week from 8 AM to midnight Eastern time. It is peer support, not a crisis line.

items.name: Nisa Homes
items.desc: Safe shelter for women and children, with locations across Canada. It is run by the Nisa Foundation. Apply through the Nisa Foundation website, or call the Nisa Helpline.

supportGroups.warningTitle: If someone checks your phone or computer
supportGroups.warningBody: The Government of Canada warns that an abuser can monitor your online activity and history, and that there is no sure way to delete all of it. If you are worried, look up help on a device somewhere else, such as at a library or a trusted friend's home.
supportGroups.warningLinkLabel: Government of Canada: plan for your safety

items.name: NEDIC (National Eating Disorder Information Centre)
items.desc: Canada's national helpline for eating disorders, run by University Health Network. Free support by phone, email and live chat. Hours change, so check the website before you call.

supportGroups.title: Finding services in Ontario
supportGroups.intro: These lines help you find local services that are not emergencies. Outside Ontario, the Government of Canada keeps a list of services for each province and territory.
supportGroups.linkLabel: See services by province and territory

items.name: 211 Ontario
items.desc: Help finding community, social and health services near you. Answered by people 24/7, in more than 150 languages.

items.name: ConnexOntario
items.desc: Free 24/7 help finding mental health, addiction and problem gambling services in Ontario.

directories.name: Khalil Center
directories.desc: Therapy and support groups for Muslims, from clinicians who work with faith rather than around it.

directories.name: Your local imam or Muslim chaplain
directories.desc: Many imams and chaplains are trained in spiritual and emotional care. Ask at your local mosque.

directories.name: Local convert support groups
directories.desc: Ask your mosque whether there is a convert group nearby. Many communities hold regular meetings where new Muslims talk through the same problems together.

reading.name: Becoming Muslim: The Lives of American Converts to Islam
reading.desc: A 2025 Yaqeen Institute report on 618 converts in the United States. It covers what helped them after conversion, such as mosques, imams and Muslim friends. It is research, not a self-help guide.

firstVisit.title: Before your first visit
firstVisit.subtitle: A few minutes of checking ahead makes the visit calmer.
firstVisit.askTitle: What to ask before you go
askItems: What time should I arrive for this prayer or Jumu'ah?
Which entrance should a first-time visitor use?
Is the women's prayer area open for this prayer?
Is there a new Muslim contact, a class, or a mentor?
Is there parking, and is there an accessible entrance?
firstVisit.scriptBody: Assalamu alaykum. I am a new Muslim and I would like to visit for the first time. Could you tell me where to enter, whether there is a new Muslim contact, and anything I should know before coming?
verifyItems: Start with the official website when a source tag is shown.
Call or email before relying on notes about classes, Jumu'ah, parking, or accessibility.
Treat a profile with no source as something you still need to verify locally.
Ask whether anything changed for Ramadan, Eid, construction, or a special event.
firstVisit.bringBody: Wear clean, modest clothes you can bow and prostrate in. A prayer mat is optional. Socks help if you feel self-conscious about taking your shoes off.
firstVisit.bringFallback: If that masjid cannot help, ask whether they know a nearby class, a chaplain, a convert group, or someone at another masjid.

qibla.learnMoreBody: Muslims everywhere pray toward the same point, the Kaaba in Mecca. Whatever country someone is praying in, the direction is shared.

asmaAlHusna.reflectionBody: The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said: "Allah has ninety-nine names. Whoever memorizes them will enter Paradise." Take your time with them.

duaDhikr.metadataDescription: A beginner's reference in English to Quranic duas, hadith duas, dhikr phrases, and where your own wording fits.
duaDhikr.title: Supplication and remembrance (dua and dhikr)
duaDhikr.subtitle: A short, source-tagged set of duas and remembrance phrases to start from. Learn a few of them properly before you add more.
usingPoints: {count} entries in total, picked to be learnable rather than exhaustive.
Quranic wording and hadith wording are labeled separately.
Your own words are welcome too, and this page marks them as yours rather than transmitted.
duaDhikr.crisisTitle: When you need more than a dua card
duaDhikr.crisisBody: If you might hurt yourself, feel unsafe, are being abused, or cannot get through the day, call emergency services, a crisis line, a clinician, or a local professional you trust. Dua and practical help work together. One does not replace the other.
duaDhikr.noArabicNote: There is no fixed Arabic wording for this one.

compactReference.title: After prayer
compactReference.body: Say SubhanAllah, Alhamdulillah, and Allahu akbar slowly. Add the full count once that feels steady.

compactReference.title: When overwhelmed
compactReference.body: Say one short dua, breathe, then do one practical thing: call someone safe, get out of danger, ask for help.

compactReference.title: Before learning
compactReference.body: Ask Allah for useful knowledge and an open heart before a class, a book, or a hard conversation.

duaDhikr.sourcesNote: The references listed here have been checked. Hadith wording, transliteration, and anything personal still need review by someone qualified.

quranStarter.metadataDescription: A beginner's Quran starter path: what to read, how to listen, what a translation is and is not, how to handle a mushaf, and a printable first week.
quranStarter.title: Quran starter path
quranStarter.subtitle: Start reading and listening without turning it into a project you can fail. Short passages, honest translations, one question at a time.
mattersMost: A small portion read with attention beats a long stretch read under pressure.
English carries the meaning across. The Arabic is the Quran.
When a verse confuses or worries you, take it to a teacher you trust.
quranStarter.translationBody: The Arabic is the revealed text. English gets you to the meaning, and it is still one person's rendering, so some of what the Arabic holds does not come across.
quranStarter.readingPathsBody: Nothing here is saved and nothing is tracked. Pick one path, read slowly, and stop before you have had too much.
quranStarter.weekBody: Print it and keep it somewhere you will see it. It does not save your progress or remind you of anything.
listening: Start with one short surah and one reciter.
Listen once without doing anything else, then listen again while you follow the translation.
If you are working on pronunciation, repeat one short phrase rather than a whole surah.
When you want your recitation corrected, get a teacher, an imam, or a class.
respect: Keep a physical mushaf in a clean, respectful place.
Ask a qualified local teacher about the wudu and purity rules for touching the Arabic text.
The same handling rules do not all apply to translations and phone apps, though treating them with care is still good adab.
Do not let the fear of getting a detail wrong stop you from reading and listening at all.

confusingVerse.title: Pause
confusingVerse.body: Do not settle the question from a screenshot, a short clip, or an argument you stumbled into online.

confusingVerse.title: Read around it
confusingVerse.body: Read the verses before and after it, then read a trusted explanation.

confusingVerse.title: Write the exact question
confusingVerse.body: Write down the verse, what bothered you about it, and what you actually want cleared up.

confusingVerse.title: Ask someone reliable
confusingVerse.body: Take it to a teacher, an imam, or a learning program that shows its sources.

quranStarter.resourcesBody: Stick to sources that name their publisher and their teachers. Anonymous quote images and debate channels are a poor way to learn the Quran.
quranStarter.sourcesNote: The Quran references, translation notes, listening guidance, and handling notes on this page have been checked. Questions about your own recitation, purity, or tafsir belong with a qualified teacher.
quranStarter.learnArabicBody: You do not need to learn the whole language to pray. Start with Al-Fatihah, the chapter recited in every rak'ah, and learn its words and what they mean. Keep praying with what you know while you do.
quranStarter.wordByWordBody: Each word with a transliteration and a translation of its meaning. The English helps you understand. The Arabic is the Quran. Read it right to left, one line a day.

salahCompanion.metadataDescription: A beginner's companion to salah in English: the shape of the prayer, the recitations you need, common worries, and sourced next steps.
salahCompanion.title: Learn to pray (salah)
salahCompanion.subtitle: A calm walk through a simple two-unit prayer, with the recitations a beginner needs and honest notes on when to go and ask someone.
mattersMost: Pray sincerely while you are still learning the words.
Get the shape of the prayer down before you chase every detail.
Ask a qualified imam about anything that turns on your own circumstances.
salahCompanion.shapeTitle: The shape of a two-unit prayer
salahCompanion.shapeBody: This is a map, not a teacher. Use it to learn the order, then ask a local imam or teacher to watch you once and correct you.
salahCompanion.recitationBody: Each card gives the Arabic, a transliteration, and the meaning. Where the text is Quran, the English is a translation of meaning to help you understand it, and the Arabic is the Quran.
salahCompanion.cannotReciteTitle: If you cannot recite Arabic yet
salahCompanion.invalidatesBody: This is an overview for beginners. The details differ between schools of law and by circumstance.
salahCompanion.correctionsTitle: Common worries, and what to do about them
askImam: Pain, disability, injury, or trauma stops you standing, bowing, sitting, or prostrating.
You do not know what to recite while your Arabic is still coming along.
You keep missing prayers and need a make-up plan you can actually follow.
Videos or different schools of law have left you with advice that contradicts itself.
Work, school, travel, family, or your own safety changes how you can pray.
salahCompanion.sourcesNote: This is a beginner companion. The references have been checked. Personal prayer rulings, school-specific details, disability accommodations, and unusual situations still need review by someone qualified.
salahCompanion.watchBody: Seeing the movements once makes the map above easier to follow. Pick one prayer from the list under the video if you only want a few minutes.
salahCompanion.phrasesVideoTitle: Learn the words, one phrase at a time
salahCompanion.phrasesVideoBody: Short lessons from Islamwise, a new Muslim project run with Green Lane Masjid. Each one says a phrase slowly and explains what it means.
salahCompanion.placementBody: Every prayer ends with a sitting. Prayers with three or four rak'ahs also have a shorter sitting after the second rak'ah.

wuduGhusl.metadataDescription: A beginner's print-friendly guide to washing before prayer: wudu, ghusl (the full-body wash), tayammum, and when to ask someone qualified.
wuduGhusl.title: Washing before prayer (wudu and ghusl)
wuduGhusl.subtitle: A simple guide to washing before prayer, made to be printed. Learn the essentials first, and take anything that depends on your own situation to a qualified teacher.
mattersMost: The water reaches everywhere it needs to.
You are washing for Allah, not out of panic.
You ask someone when a medical, work, or family situation makes this complicated.
wuduGhusl.wuduTitle: Washing before prayer (wudu), step by step
wuduGhusl.wuduBody: Wudu is the partial washing you normally do before prayer. Quran 5:6 sets out which parts are washed and which are wiped, and beginner guides fill in the practical order.
wuduGhusl.ghuslTitle: The full-body wash (ghusl), step by step
wuduGhusl.ghuslBody: Ghusl is the full-body wash. Keep it modest and keep it simple: intend it, clean what needs cleaning, and make sure water reaches your whole body.
wuduGhusl.correctionsTitle: Common worries, and what to do about them
askQualified: A medical condition, a wound, a disability, or severe dryness makes using water difficult.
You are unsure about menstruation, postpartum bleeding, discharge, or rulings around intimacy.
Your job, school, travel, or family situation makes purification hard to manage.
You feel stuck repeating wudu or ghusl because of anxiety.
wuduGhusl.sourcesNote: This is a beginner tool. Some purification details differ between schools of law, and your own situation is worth going over with a qualified local imam or scholar.

getHelp.title: Get help
getHelp.subtitle: Ask a question, ask for a mentor, find events near you, or tell us about a concern. A small team reads every request.

crisis.text: If you are in danger, call 911. For a mental health crisis, call or text 9-8-8.
crisis.linkLabel: More support on the mental health page

placeholderNotice.title: The form is still being set up
placeholderNotice.body: The request form and the email addresses on this page are not working yet. Until they are, your local masjid is a good place to ask, and the crisis lines above are there if you need help now.

whatFor.title: What you can ask us for

items.title: Ask a question
items.body: Anything you are unsure about, from prayer to telling your family. If we are not the right people to answer, we will tell you who is.

items.title: Ask for a mentor
items.body: A trained volunteer, usually of the same gender, who checks in with you and helps with the basics.

items.title: Events and community
items.body: Classes, new Muslim get-togethers and masjids near you.

items.title: Report a concern
items.body: Something about a mentor, a group or an admin that did not feel right.

form.title: Send a request
form.body: The form opens on Google Forms in a new tab.
asks: The language you would like to use
Whether you would prefer a mentor of the same gender
How you would like us to contact you
A message, if you want to add one
A line where you agree to us using your answers to reply to you
form.asksNote: That is all. We only ask what we need to reply and, if you want one, to find you a mentor.

whoReads.title: Who reads it
whoReads.body: One or two volunteer coordinators read every request from one shared inbox. Nobody else sees it. If you ask for a mentor, the coordinator tells you about the match first and passes on only what the mentor needs, once you agree.
whoReads.response: We aim to reply within 48 to 72 hours. That is a target, not a promise. Replies can be slower over holidays and in Ramadan.
whoReads.mentoringLinkLabel: How mentoring works and our conduct standards

privacy.title: Your privacy
items: A help request tells us that you are Muslim or thinking about Islam, so we treat it as sensitive.
Only the coordinators read it. We do not share it with your family, a masjid or anyone else without asking you first.
The form is run by Google, which may store your answers outside Canada.
We aim to delete a request six months after we close it.
If someone else checks your phone or computer, you can send the form from another device, such as a library computer, and give us a contact method only you can see.

report.title: Report a mentor, group or admin
report.body: Tell us if a mentor, a group member or an admin asks you for money, proposes marriage, pushes you to join something, or makes you feel unsafe. Your report goes to the coordinators, never to the person you are reporting.
report.scamNote: If someone asked you for money or you think you were scammed, you can also report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501.

contact.title: Rather send an email?
contact.body: You can write to us instead of using the form. The same coordinators read this inbox.

guideLink.label: How to ask for help

getHelp.sourcesNote: These sources back how the form is set up and how your details are handled. The reply target and the retention period are our own targets.

communityGroups.title: Community groups
communityGroups.subtitle: Reminders, local news and the company of other new Muslims, set up so you choose how much of yourself to share.

placeholderNotice.title: These links are still being set up
placeholderNotice.body: The channel link and the group list on this page are not live yet. We will add them once the admins are in place.

channel.title: Our WhatsApp Channel
channel.body: A one-way channel for reminders, new pages on the site and events. Only admins post, and other followers cannot see your phone number.

groups.title: Local groups
groups.body: Small groups by city or region where you can ask questions and meet people. Admins approve every new member.
groups.emptyState: Groups will be listed here once admins are in place.
groups.joinNote: Joining a group shows your phone number to the group admins, and other members may see it too.

reveals.title: What each option shows about you

items.name: Channel
items.body: Your phone number stays private. An admin can see it only if they already have you saved as a contact. Only you can see which channels you follow, and followers cannot message each other there.

items.name: Group
items.body: Admins see your number, and other members may see it too. Anyone in the group can message you.

items.name: Community
items.body: A community is a set of linked groups. Your number is visible to its admins and to people who already have it, rather than to every member.

reveals.usernameNote: WhatsApp is slowly rolling out usernames, which hide your number from people who do not already have it. You may not have them yet.

safety.title: If you are keeping your conversion private
safety.body: Follow the channel rather than joining a group, because the channel keeps your number hidden. Group names and messages can show up in your notifications, so think about who can see your phone before you join anything.

rules.title: Group rules
rules.intro: Everyone who joins agrees to these. Admins remove anyone who breaks them.
items: No asking for money, selling or fundraising.
No marriage proposals or matchmaking.
No private messages to members who have not asked for them.
No forwarding members' names, numbers, photos or messages outside the group.
Nobody is added without choosing to join. We share the link and you decide.
rules.admins: Admins are volunteers in a set role, not named individuals. They approve new members, remove and report scam accounts, and pass any safety concern to the coordinators.

report.title: Reporting a problem
report.body: If someone in a group or the channel asks you for money, proposes marriage, messages you privately without being asked, or shares your details, tell us. Reports go to the coordinators. You can also report and block the account inside WhatsApp.
report.linkLabel: Go to the Get help page

redFlags.prompt: Know the warning signs of scams and pressure in community spaces.
redFlags.label: Red flags and staying safe

communityGroups.sourcesNote: What each option shows comes from WhatsApp's own help pages. WhatsApp can change how these features work, so check its help centre if you are unsure.

events.title: Events
events.subtitle: New Muslim get-togethers, classes and open events at masjids across Canada.
events.intro: Each event is run by its organiser, not by us. Details can change, so check with the organiser before you go.
events.noRegistration: There is no registration on this site. To sign up, use the organiser's own page.

empty.title: No events listed right now
empty.body: We add events once organisers confirm them. Your local masjid may keep its own calendar, and if you know of an event for new Muslims, you can tell us about it.

tellUs.prompt: Know of an event that would suit new Muslims?
tellUs.label: Tell us about an event
